title: حِكَايَةُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
part: Night 47 · King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 360–368 (Night 47, continuing directly from nights-46), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm exactly as Macnaghten prints it. Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition's Middle Arabic forms and its occasional compositor's slips, is preserved unaltered; a few genuinely obscure or corrupt-looking forms are vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes rather than silently repaired. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 47 continues the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. Prince Sharkān, lost at night in the Byzantine lands, watches the girl he has seen throw the old woman Dhāt al-Dawāhī, then rides at her, swears the oath she demands, and wrestles her himself: she throws him twice, spares him, and lets him follow her to a monastery by the river, where she tells him she knows who he is. The night breaks off as she says she longs to have Sharkān in her hands. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّابِعَةُ وَالْأَرْبَعُونَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sābiʿatu wa-al-arbaʿūn
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the seventh and the forty,
sentences.i: And when it was the forty-seventh night,
sentences.n: The opening formula of every night. The ordinal is built the Arabic way, units before tens: "the seventh and the forty". كَانَتْ is used in its full sense, "there came", so اللَّيْلَةُ is its subject; the final كَانَتِ takes a kasra only to bridge into the article that follows.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الْجَارِيَةَ لَمَّا قَالَتْ لِذَاتِ الدَّوَاهِي بِحَقِّ الْمَسِيحِ أَتُصَارِعِينَنِي حَقِيقَةً أَمْ تَمْزَحِينَ مَعِي قَالَتْ لَهَا بَلْ أُصَارِعُكِ حَقِيقَةً وَشَرْكَانُ يَنْظُرُ إِلَيْهِنَّ قَالَتْ لَهَا قُومِي لِلصِّرَاعِ إِنْ كَانَ لَكِ قُوَّةٌ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-jāriyata lammā qālat li-Dhāti al-Dawāhī bi-ḥaqqi al-Masīḥi a-tuṣāriʿīnanī ḥaqīqatan am tamzaḥīna maʿī qālat lahā bal uṣāriʿuki ḥaqīqatan wa-Sharkānu yanẓuru ilayhinna qālat lahā qūmī li-al-ṣirāʿi in kāna laki quwwatun
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king, the happy, that the girl, when she said to Mistress-of-Calamities, "By the right of the Messiah, are you wrestling me in truth, or are you jesting with me?" — she said to her, "Nay, I wrestle you in truth," while Sharkān was looking at them; she said to her, "Arise for the wrestling, if there is to you strength."
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when the girl said to Dhāt al-Dawāhī, "By the Messiah's right, will you wrestle me in earnest, or are you making a jest of me?" the old woman answered, "No, I will wrestle you in earnest," while Sharkān watched them. Then the girl said, "Rise and wrestle, if you have any strength."
sentences.n: Every speaker here is "she", so keep track: the first qālat after the oath is the girl challenging the old woman; the second qālat lahā is the old woman answering; the last is the girl again. The that-clause opened by أَنَّ is never completed in a grammatical way; the narrative simply runs on. ذَاتُ الدَّوَاهِي, "Mistress of Calamities", is the old woman's name. The edition prints السعيدان as one word (al-saʿīd with anna fused on); it is kept run together exactly as printed. إِنْ كَانَ لَكِ قُوَّةٌ is the Arabic "if there is to you strength", that is, "if you have strength".

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتِ الْعَجُوزُ مِنْهَا ذَلِكَ اغْتَاظَتْ غَيْظًا شَدِيدًا وَقَامَ شَعْرُ بَدَنِهَا كَأَنَّهُ شَعْرُ قُنْفُذٍ ثُمَّ وَثَبَتْ وَقَامَتْ إِلَيْهَا الْجَارِيَةُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿati al-ʿajūzu minhā dhālika ightāẓat ghayẓan shadīdan wa-qāma shaʿru badanihā kaʾannahu shaʿru qunfudhin thumma wathabat wa-qāmat ilayhā al-jāriyatu
sentences.l: And when the old woman heard that from her, she was enraged with a severe rage, and the hair of her body stood up, as if it were the hair of a hedgehog; then she sprang up, and the girl rose to her.
sentences.i: When the old woman heard this from her, she was seized with a violent rage, and the hair on her body bristled like a hedgehog's quills. Then she sprang up, and the girl rose to face her.
sentences.n: The edition itself prints a damma on the qāf of قُنفذ; it is kept, and the rest of the word is pointed around it. قُنْفُذ is the hedgehog. قَامَ إِلَى is "rise toward", that is, to face someone.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهَا الْعَجُوزُ وَحَقِّ الْمَسِيحِ لَمْ أُصَارِعْكِ إِلَّا وَأَنَا عُرْيَانَةٌ يَا فَاجِرَةُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahā al-ʿajūzu wa-ḥaqqi al-Masīḥi lam uṣāriʿki illā wa-anā ʿuryānatun yā fājiratu
sentences.l: And the old woman said to her: By the right of the Messiah, I do not wrestle you except while I am naked, O depraved one!
sentences.i: Then the old woman said to her, "By the Messiah's right, I will wrestle you only if I am stripped naked, you shameless wretch!"
sentences.n: لَمْ with the jussive normally negates the past, but here it looks forward: "I will not wrestle you unless …". That is a Middle Arabic use of lam where Classical would say lan; we pointed what the text says. إِلَّا وَأَنَا عُرْيَانَةٌ is "except while I am naked", a circumstantial clause introduced by wa-. The oath وَحَقِّ الْمَسِيحِ takes the genitive.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْعَجُوزَ أَخَذَتْ مِنْدِيلَ حَرِيرٍ وَفَكَّتْ لِبَاسَهَا وَأَدْخَلَتْ يَدَيْهَا تَحْتَ ثِيَابِهَا وَنَزَعَتْهَا مِنْ فَوْقِ جَسَدِهَا وَلَمَّتِ الْمِنْدِيلَ وَشَدَّتْهُ فِي وَسَطِهَا فَصَارَتْ كَأَنَّهَا عِفْرِيتَةٌ مَعْطَاءُ أَوْحَيَّةٌ رَقْطَاءُ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-ʿajūza akhadhat mindīla ḥarīrin wa-fakkat libāsahā wa-adkhalat yadayhā taḥta thiyābihā wa-nazaʿathā min fawqi jasadihā wa-lammati al-mindīla wa-shaddathu fī wasaṭihā fa-ṣārat kaʾannahā ʿifrītatun maʿṭāʾu awḥayyatun raqṭāʾu
sentences.l: Then the old woman took a kerchief of silk, and loosened her undergarment, and put her hands in under her clothes and pulled them off from upon her body; and she gathered up the kerchief and bound it on her middle; and she became as if she were a she-ʿifrīt, hairless, or a snake, speckled.
sentences.i: Then the old woman took a silk kerchief and undid her drawers, thrust her hands under her clothes and stripped them off her body; then she bunched up the kerchief and tied it round her waist, and she looked like some bald she-demon, or a speckled serpent.
sentences.n: مَعْطَاءُ is obscure. Lane has أَمْعَطُ, feminine مَعْطَاءُ, for one bare of hair; we read it so, since it is paired with رَقْطَاءُ, "speckled", another colour-and-surface adjective of the same pattern. It is a reading, not a certainty. أَوْحَيَّةٌ is printed as one word for أَوْ حَيَّةٌ, "or a snake"; kept fused. A عِفْرِيت is a powerful, malign jinn, here in the feminine. لِبَاس can mean any garment, including the drawers worn beneath; we take it so, since she then reaches under her clothes.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ انْحَنَتْ عَلَى الْجَارِيَةِ وَقَالَتْ لَهَا افْعَلِي كَفِعْلِي كُلِّ هَذَا وَشَرْكَانُ يَنْظُرُ إِلَيْهِمَا ثُمَّ إِنَّ شَرْكَانَ صَارَ يَتَأَمَّلُ فِي تَشْوِيهِ صُورَةِ الْعَجُوزِ وَيَضْحَكُ
sentences.tr: thumma inḥanat ʿalā al-jāriyati wa-qālat lahā ifʿalī ka-fiʿlī kulli hādhā wa-Sharkānu yanẓuru ilayhimā thumma inna Sharkāna ṣāra yataʾammalu fī tashwīhi ṣūrati al-ʿajūzi wa-yaḍḥaku
sentences.l: Then she bent over the girl and said to her: Do like my doing, all of this — and Sharkān was looking at the two of them. Then Sharkān began to contemplate the disfigurement of the old woman's form, and to laugh.
sentences.i: Then she bent toward the girl and said, "Do as I have done, all of it!" — with Sharkān watching the two of them. And Sharkān fell to gazing at the old woman's grotesque figure, and laughed.
sentences.n: Whether كُلِّ هَذَا belongs to her speech ("do as I have done, all this") or is the narrator's aside is not settled by the print; we read it as part of her speech, in apposition to the genitive فِعْلِي. صَارَ followed by an imperfect verb is "began to, fell to".

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْعَجُوزَ لَمَّا فَعَلَتْ ذَلِكَ قَامَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ عَلَى مَهَلٍ وَأَخَذَتْ فُوطَةً يَمَانِيَّةً وَثَنَّتْهَا مَرَّتَيْنِ وَشَمَّرَتْ سَرَاوِيلَهَا
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-ʿajūza lammā faʿalat dhālika qāmati al-jāriyatu ʿalā mahalin wa-akhadhat fūṭatan yamāniyyatan wa-thannathā marratayni wa-shammarat sarāwīlahā
sentences.l: Then, the old woman, when she had done that — the girl rose at leisure, and took a Yemeni waist-wrap, and doubled it twice, and tucked up her trousers.
sentences.i: When the old woman had done all this, the girl rose without haste, took a Yemeni waist-wrap and folded it double, and tucked up her trousers.
sentences.n: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْعَجُوزَ … قَامَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ: the إِنَّ is left without a predicate of its own, and the sentence simply restarts after the لَمَّا clause. This is loose, but common in this register. The edition prints a shadda on the nūn of وَثَنَّتْهَا; it is kept. A فُوطَة is a waist-wrap or cloth, and ثَنَّى is "to double, fold in two". سَرَاوِيل is the trousers or drawers, a diptote.

sentences.t: فَبَانَ لَهَا سَاقَانِ مِنَ الْمَرْمَرِ وَفَوْقَهُمَا كَثِيبٌ مِنَ الْبَلُّورِ نَاعِمٌ مُرَبْرَبٌ وَبَطْنٌ يَفُوحُ الْمِسْكُ مِنْ أَعْكَانِهِ كَأَنَّهُ مُصَفَّحٌ بِشَقَائِقِ النُّعْمَانِ وَصَلَ رَفِيهِ نَهْدَانِ كَفَحْلَيْ رُمَّانٍ
sentences.tr: fa-bāna lahā sāqāni mina al-marmari wa-fawqahumā kathībun mina al-ballūri nāʿimun murabrabun wa-baṭnun yafūḥu al-misku min aʿkānihi kaʾannahu muṣaffaḥun bi-shaqāʾiqi al-Nuʿmāni waṣala rafīhi nahdāni ka-faḥlay rummānin
sentences.l: And there appeared, of hers, two legs of marble, and above them a dune of crystal, soft, plump; and a belly, the musk wafts from its folds, as if it were plated with anemones; [corrupt: waṣala rafīhi] two breasts like two stallions of pomegranate.
sentences.i: Her legs showed bare, two columns of marble, and above them a dune of crystal, soft and plump; and a belly from whose folds the scent of musk breathed, as if overlaid with anemones; and on her chest two breasts like a pair of pomegranates.
sentences.n: لَهَا after بَانَ is the possessive dative: "there appeared to her" for "hers appeared". كَثِيب is a sand-dune, a common figure for a woman's hips and mound; here it sits above the legs, so it means just that. مُرَبْرَب, "plump", is our best reading of an uncommon word. شَقَائِق النُّعْمَان is the red anemone; the phrase has nothing to do with King al-Nuʿmān of the story. The words وصل رفيه are printed so and are evidently corrupt; the sense wanted is something like وَصَدْرٌ فِيهِ, "and a chest, in which (were) two breasts", but we may not change letters, so they are pointed as printed (waṣala rafīhi) and left without meaning; the idiomatic line supplies the probable sense. فَحْلَا رُمَّانٍ, literally "two stallions of pomegranate", means two choice pomegranates, the "male" being the finest; it is a stock image of firm round breasts.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ انْحَنَتْ عَلَيْهَا الْعَجُوزُ وَتَمَاسَكَا بِبَعْضِهِمَا فَرَفَعَ شَرْكَانُ رَأْسَهُ إِلَى السَّمَاءِ وَدَعَا اللَّهَ أَنَّ الْجَارِيَةَ تَغْلِبُ الْعَجُوزَ
sentences.tr: thumma inḥanat ʿalayhā al-ʿajūzu wa-tamāsakā bi-baʿḍihimā fa-rafaʿa Sharkānu raʾsahu ilā al-samāʾi wa-daʿā Allāha anna al-jāriyata taghlibu al-ʿajūza
sentences.l: Then the old woman bent over her, and the two gripped one another, by some-of-the-two (each to the other); and Sharkān raised his head to the sky and called on God that the girl overcome the old woman.
sentences.i: Then the old woman bent over her, and the two locked together; and Sharkān lifted his head to heaven and prayed to God that the girl might throw the old woman.
sentences.n: تَمَاسَكَا بِبَعْضِهِمَا, literally "they held fast with some of them", is the reciprocal "each held the other"; the بِـ is the one tamāsaka takes for what is gripped. دَعَا اللَّهَ أَنَّ الْجَارِيَةَ تَغْلِبُ is Middle Arabic: Classical would use أَنْ with the subjunctive ("that she overcome") rather than أَنَّ with an indicative.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ تَحْتَ الْعَجُوزِ وَوَضَعَتْ يَدَهَا الشِّمَالَ فِي شِقَّتِهَا وَيَدَهَا الْيُمْنَى فِي رَقَبَتِهَا مَعَ حَلْقِهَا وَرَفَعَتْهَا عَلَى يَدَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-dakhalati al-jāriyatu taḥta al-ʿajūzi wa-waḍaʿat yadahā al-shimāla fī shiqqatihā wa-yadahā al-yumnā fī raqabatihā maʿa ḥalqihā wa-rafaʿathā ʿalā yadayhā
sentences.l: And the girl went in under the old woman, and put her hand, the left, in her cleft, and her hand, the right, on her neck together with her throat, and lifted her up on her two hands.
sentences.i: So the girl got in beneath the old woman, set her left hand between her thighs and her right hand at her neck and throat, and heaved her up on her arms.
sentences.n: شِقَّتِهَا is uncertain. شِقَّة is "a side, a portion", but with one hand low and the other at the throat the hold points to the crotch, so we take it as "her cleft"; the print may intend شَقَّتِهَا from شَقّ, "cleft". الشِّمَال, "the left", is used here as a noun in apposition to يَدَهَا, in the gender-loose way of this register.

sentences.t: فَانْفَلَتَتِ الْعَجُوزُ مِنْ يَدَيْهَا وَأَرَادَتِ الْخَلَاصَ فَوَقَعَتْ عَلَى ظَهْرِهَا فَارْتَفَعَتْ رِجْلَاهَا إِلَى فَوْقٍ فَبَانَ فِى الْقَمَرِ شِعْرَتُهَا فَضَرَطَتْ ضَرْطَتَيْنِ عَفَّرَتْ أَحَدُهُمَا فِى الْأَرْضِ وَدَخَّنَتِ الْأُخْرَى فِى السَّمَاءِ
sentences.tr: fa-infalatati al-ʿajūzu min yadayhā wa-arādati al-khalāṣa fa-waqaʿat ʿalā ẓahrihā fa-irtafaʿat rijlāhā ilā fawqin fa-bāna fī al-qamari shiʿratuhā fa-ḍaraṭat ḍarṭatayni ʿaffarat aḥaduhumā fī al-arḍi wa-dakhkhanati al-ukhrā fī al-samāʾi
sentences.l: And the old woman slipped from her hands and wanted release, and fell on her back, and her two legs rose to above; and there appeared in the moon her pubic hair; and she farted two farts: one of them dusted the ground, and the other smoked in the sky.
sentences.i: But the old woman slipped from her hands and, struggling to get free, fell on her back, her legs flying up in the air, and her pubic hair showed in the moonlight; and she let fly two farts, one that raised the dust on the ground and one that sent smoke up into the sky.
sentences.n: شِعْرَة is the pubic hair, the mons. فِى الْقَمَرِ is "in the moon", that is, by moonlight. The two farts are described without a connecting word, each in its own clause: عَفَّرَتْ is "to strew with dust" and دَخَّنَتْ "to send up smoke". The edition prints أَحَدُهُمَا, the masculine "one of them", though ضَرْطَة is feminine (Classical would have إِحْدَاهُمَا); read as printed. The edition spells في as فى here and elsewhere; kept.

sentences.t: فَضَحِكَ شَرْكَانُ عَلَيْهَا حَتَّى وَقَعَ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ ثُمَّ قَامَ وَسَلَّ حُسَامَهُ وَالْتَفَتَ يَمِينًا وَشِمَالًا فَلَمْ يَرَ أَحَدًا غَيْرَ الْعَجُوزِ مَرْمِيَّةً عَلَى ظَهْرِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-ḍaḥika Sharkānu ʿalayhā ḥattā waqaʿa ʿalā al-arḍi thumma qāma wa-salla ḥusāmahu wa-iltafata yamīnan wa-shimālan fa-lam yara aḥadan ghayra al-ʿajūzi marmiyyatan ʿalā ẓahrihā
sentences.l: And Sharkān laughed at her until he fell upon the ground; then he rose, and drew his sword, and turned right and left, and saw no one other than the old woman, thrown on her back.
sentences.i: Sharkān laughed at her until he fell to the ground. Then he got up, drew his sword, and looked to right and left, and saw no one but the old woman lying flung on her back.
sentences.n: ضَحِكَ عَلَى is "laugh at". مَرْمِيَّةً is accusative as a circumstantial word describing the old woman, "lying thrown".

sentences.t: فَقَالَ شَرْكَانُ فِي نَفْسِهِ مَاكَذَبَ مَنْ سَمَّاكِ ذَاتَ الدَّوَاهِي هَذَا وَأَنْتِ تَعْرِفُ قُوَّتَهَا مَعَ غَيْرِكِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Sharkānu fī nafsihi mākadhaba man sammāki Dhāta al-Dawāhī hādhā wa-anti taʿrifu quwwatahā maʿa ghayriki
sentences.l: And Sharkān said in himself: He did not lie who named you Mistress-of-Calamities — this! — and you know her strength with other-than-you.
sentences.i: Sharkān said to himself, "He told no lie who named you Dhāt al-Dawāhī, the Mistress of Calamities — this! — and you knew the girl's strength against others!"
sentences.n: The sense of this speech is uncertain. Sharkān addresses the old woman as "you" (feminine), yet speaks of "her strength"; the most natural reading takes "her" as the girl, so that the old woman, who knew how the girl fared against other opponents, still took her on. It is a reading, not a certainty. The print has تعرف without the feminine ending -īna; we point it تَعْرِفُ and read it as "you know" (a slip or Middle Arabic dropping of the ending). مَاكَذَبَ is printed as one word, mā kadhaba; kept. سَمَّى takes two accusatives, "named you X".

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَقَرَّبَ مِنْهُمَا لِيَسْمَعَ مَا يَجْرِي بَيْنَهُمَا فَأَقْبَلَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ وَرَمَتْ عَلَيْهَا مُلَاءَةً مِنْ حَرِيرٍ رَفِيعَةً وَأَلْبَسَتْهَا ثِيَابَهَا وَاعْتَذَرَتْ لَهَا وَقَالَتْ لَهَا يَاسِتِّي ذَاتَ الدَّوَاهِي مَا أَرَدْتُ إِلَّاصَرْعَكِ لَاجَمِيعَ مَا حَصَلَ لَكِ وَلَكِنْ إِنَّكِ انْفَلَتِّ مِنْ بَيْنِ يَدَيَّ فَالْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ عَلَى السَّلَامَةِ
sentences.tr: thumma taqarraba minhumā li-yasmaʿa mā yajrī baynahumā fa-aqbalati al-jāriyatu wa-ramat ʿalayhā mulāʾatan min ḥarīrin rafīʿatan wa-albasathā thiyābahā wa-iʿtadharat lahā wa-qālat lahā yāsittī Dhāta al-Dawāhī mā aradtu illāṣarʿaki lājamīʿa mā ḥaṣala laki wa-lākin innaki infalatti min bayni yadayya fa-al-ḥamdu li-Allāhi ʿalā al-salāmati
sentences.l: Then he drew near to the two of them, that he might hear what passed between them; and the girl came forward, and threw over her a sheet of silk, fine, and clothed her in her clothes, and made excuse to her; and she said to her: My lady, Mistress-of-Calamities, I wanted nothing but your throwing, not all that has befallen you; but you slipped from between my hands; so praise be to God for safety.
sentences.i: Then he moved closer to them to hear what passed between them. The girl came forward, threw a fine silk wrap over the old woman, dressed her in her clothes and made her excuses. "My lady, Dhāt al-Dawāhī," she said, "I meant only to throw you, not for all this to befall you; but you slipped from between my hands. Praise be to God that you are safe!"
sentences.n: Three words are printed run together and kept so: يَاسِتِّي (yā + sitt-ī, "my lady"), إِلَّاصَرْعَكِ (illā + ṣarʿaki, "nothing but your throwing") and لَاجَمِيعَ (lā + jamīʿa, "not all of"). The shadda and kasra on the final ت of انْفَلَتِّ are the edition's own; the form is the feminine "you slipped" (infalatti), the root t and the ending -ti merged. The edition also prints a damma on the م of مُلَاءَة, kept. الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ عَلَى السَّلَامَةِ is the stock "thank God for your safety". وَاعْتَذَرَتْ لَهَا is "she apologised to her".

sentences.t: فَلَمْ تَرُدَّ عَلَيْهَا جَوَابًا وَقَامَتْ تَمْشِي مِنْ خَجَلِهَا وَلَمْ تَزَلْ مَاشِيَةً إِلَى أَنْ غَابَتْ عَنِ الْبَصَرِ وَصَارَ الْجَوَارِي مُكَتَّفَاتٍ مَرْمِيَّاتٍ وَالْجَارِيَةُ وَاقِفَةٌ وَحْدَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lam tarudda ʿalayhā jawāban wa-qāmat tamshī min khajalihā wa-lam tazal māshiyatan ilā an ghābat ʿan al-baṣari wa-ṣāra al-jawārī mukattafātin marmiyyātin wa-al-jāriyatu wāqifatun waḥdahā
sentences.l: And she did not return to her an answer, and rose, walking from her shame, and did not cease walking until she vanished from the sight; and the slave-girls became bound-ones, thrown-ones, and the girl standing alone.
sentences.i: The old woman gave her no answer, but got up and walked off in her shame, and went on walking until she was lost to sight. The other girls lay bound and cast down, and the girl was left standing alone.
sentences.n: مِنْ خَجَلِهَا: مِنْ gives the cause, "out of her shame". لَمْ تَزَلْ مَاشِيَةً is "she did not cease walking". The last clause is not explained by anything before it: the other girls are described as مُكَتَّفَات, "with arms bound", and مَرْمِيَّات, "flung down"; we read the plurals as the girls' states after the bout, and the print gives no more.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ شَرْكَانُ فِي نَفْسِهِ لِكُلِّ رِزْقٍ سَبَبٌ مَا وَقَعَ عَلَيَّ النَّوْمُ وَسَارَبِي الْجَوَادُ إِلَى هَذَا الْمَكَانِ إِلَّا لِبَخْتِي فَلَعَلَّ هَذِهِ الْجَارِيَةَ وَمَا مَعَهَا تَكُونُ غَنِيمَةً لِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Sharkānu fī nafsihi li-kulli rizqin sababun mā waqaʿa ʿalayya al-nawmu wa-sāra bī al-jawādu ilā hādhā al-makāni illā li-bakhtī fa-laʿalla hādhihi al-jāriyata wa-mā maʿahā takūnu ghanīmatan lī
sentences.l: So Sharkān said in himself: For every provision a cause; sleep did not fall upon me and the steed went with me to this place except for my luck; so perhaps this girl and what is with her will be a booty for me.
sentences.i: Then Sharkān said to himself: Every livelihood has its cause. Sleep would not light upon me, and my steed has borne me to this place for no reason but my good fortune. Perhaps this girl and those with her will prove a prize for me.
sentences.n: وَسَارَبِي is printed as one word (wa + sāra + bī, "and went with me"); it is kept run together and pointed as the three pieces it is. لِكُلِّ رِزْقٍ سَبَبٌ is a saying: "for every provision there is a cause". بَخْت, "luck", is a Persian loan. After لَعَلَّ the noun is accusative (الْجَارِيَةَ), and the singular verb تَكُونُ then agrees with the girl alone, though "what is with her" is added to her.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ عَمَدَ إِلَى جَوَادِهِ وَرَكِبَهُ وَلَكَزَهُ فَقَرَّبَهُ كَالسَّهْمِ إِذَا فَرَّ مِنَ الْقَوْسِ وَبِيَدِهِ حُسَامُهُ مُجَرَّدٌ مِنْ قِرَابِهِ وَصَاحَ اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu ʿamada ilā jawādihi wa-rakibahu wa-lakazahu fa-qarrabahu ka-al-sahmi idhā farra mina al-qawsi wa-biyadihi ḥusāmuhu mujarradun min qirābihi wa-ṣāḥa Allāhu akbar
sentences.l: Then indeed he made for his steed and mounted it and jabbed it, and he made it gallop like the arrow when it flees from the bow, and in his hand his sword drawn from its scabbard; and he cried out: God is greatest.
sentences.i: Then he went to his horse, mounted, and spurred it, and it flew like an arrow loosed from the bow, with his sword bare of its scabbard in his hand; and he cried out: God is greatest!
sentences.n: فَقَرَّبَهُ: taqrīb is the name of a horse's gait, a fast, bounding canter, so we read "he put it to a gallop". The clause وَبِيَدِهِ حُسَامُهُ مُجَرَّدٌ is a circumstantial clause ("his sword being drawn in his hand"). اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ is the Muslim war-cry.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتْهُ الْجَارِيَةُ نَهَضَتْ قَائِمَةً وَحَطَّتْ قَدَمَيْهَا عَلَى جَانِبِ النَّهْرِ وَكَانَ عَرْضُهُ سِتَّةَ أَذْرُعٍ بِذِرَاعِ الْعَمَلِ وَوَثَبَتْ فَصَارَتْ فِى الْجَانِبِ الْآخَرِ وَقَامَتْ عَلَى حَيْلِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾathu al-jāriyatu nahaḍat qāʾimatan wa-ḥaṭṭat qadamayhā ʿalā jānibi al-nahri wa-kāna ʿarḍuhu sittata adhruʿin bi-dhirāʿi al-ʿamali wa-wathabat fa-ṣārat fī al-jānibi al-ākhari wa-qāmat ʿalā ḥaylihā
sentences.l: And when the girl saw him, she rose up standing, and set her two feet on the side of the river — and its breadth was six cubits by the cubit of the work — and leapt, and so became on the other side, and stood upon her strength.
sentences.i: When the girl saw him she sprang upright, planted her feet on the edge of the river, which was six cubits wide by the builders' measure, and leapt across to the far bank, and stood her ground.
sentences.n: حَيْلِهَا is obscure. Lane gives ḥayl as strength or power, so عَلَى حَيْلِهَا is read as "on her own strength", that is, firmly on her own feet; this is our reading, not a certainty. ذِرَاعُ الْعَمَلِ, "the cubit of work", is taken as the working or builders' cubit, the standard one. The girl wrestles and leaps across a six-cubit river: the text wants you to see that she is no ordinary captive.

sentences.t: وَنَادَتْ بِرَفِيعِ صَوْتِهَا مَنْ أَنْتَ يَاهَذَا فَقَدْ كُنْتَ قَاطِعًا سُرُورَنَا وَحِينَ قَهَرْتَ حُسَامَكَ كَأَنَّكَ قَدْ حَمَلْتَ عَلَى عَسْكَرٍ
sentences.tr: wa-nādat bi-rafīʿi ṣawtihā man anta yā hādhā fa-qad kunta qāṭiʿan surūranā wa-ḥīna qaharta ḥusāmaka kaʾannaka qad ḥamalta ʿalā ʿaskar
sentences.l: And she called out with the raised-one of her voice: Who are you, you there? For you were cutting off our delight, and when you overpowered your sword — as though you had charged upon an army.
sentences.i: And she cried out at the top of her voice: Who are you, sir? You have cut short our pleasure, and the way you flourished your sword, you might have been charging an army!
sentences.n: يَاهَذَا is printed as one word, yā + hādhā, "you there". قَهَرْتَ حُسَامَكَ is strange: qahara is "to overpower", and "you overpowered your sword" can only mean something like "you mastered / wielded it". The verb شَهَرَ, "to draw, brandish a sword", would suit the scene perfectly and is easy to confuse with it, so the text may be slightly corrupt; we point what is printed and translate the likely sense "flourished".

sentences.t: مِنْ أَيْنَ أَنْتَ وَأَىَّ أَيْنَ تُرِيدُ فَاصْدُقْ فِي مَقَالِكَ فَإِنَّ الصِّدْقَ أَنْفَعُ لَكَ وَلَا تَكْذِبْ فَإِنَّ الْكَذِبَ مِنْ أَخْلَاقِ اللِّئَامِ
sentences.tr: min ayna anta wa-ayya ayna turīdu fa-uṣduq fī maqālika fa-inna al-ṣidqa anfaʿu laka wa-lā takdhib fa-inna al-kadhiba min akhlāqi al-liʾām
sentences.l: From where are you, and which where do you want? So be truthful in your speech, for truth is more profitable to you, and do not lie, for lying is of the characters of the base-ones.
sentences.i: Where are you from, and whither are you bound? Speak the truth, for truth serves you better; and do not lie, for lying is the way of base men.
sentences.n: وَأَىَّ أَيْنَ تُرِيدُ is a doubled question word, "which where", i.e. "to what place"; the edition spells أي with ى. We read أَىَّ as accusative, the object of تُرِيدُ. The girl speaks in short balanced clauses (فَاصْدُقْ … فَإِنَّ … وَلَا تَكْذِبْ … فَإِنَّ …), the neat style of a moral maxim.

sentences.t: وَلَاشَكَّ أَنَّكَ تِهْتَ فِي هَذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ عَنِ الطَّرِيقِ حَتَّى جِئْتَ إِلَى هَذَا الْمَكَانِ الَّذِي خَلَاصُكَ فِيهِ أَكْبَرُ الْغَنِيمَاتِ وَأَنْتَ الْآنَ فِي مَرْجٍ لَوْ صَرَخْنَا فِيهِ صَرْخَةً وَاحِدَةً لَجَاءَ إِلَيْنَا أَرْبَعَةُ آلَافِ بِطْرِيقٍ
sentences.tr: wa-lā shakka annaka tihta fī hādhihi al-laylati ʿani al-ṭarīqi ḥattā jiʾta ilā hādhā al-makāni alladhī khalāṣuka fīhi akbaru al-ghanīmāti wa-anta al-āna fī marjin law ṣarakhnā fīhi ṣarkhatan wāḥidatan la-jāʾa ilaynā arbaʿatu ālāfi biṭrīq
sentences.l: And no doubt that you went astray in this night from the road until you came to this place, which your deliverance in it is the greatest of the booties; and you are now in a meadow, if we cried out in it one cry, there would come to us four thousand patricians.
sentences.i: Without doubt you lost your way tonight and strayed to this place, where escaping with your life would be the greatest gain; for you stand now in a meadow where, if we raised a single cry, four thousand patricians would come running to us.
sentences.n: وَلَاشَكَّ is printed as one word, wa + lā + shakk. تِهْتَ is tihta, from tāha yatīhu "to lose one's way". The relative clause الَّذِي خَلَاصُكَ فِيهِ أَكْبَرُ الْغَنِيمَاتِ is hard; literally "in which your deliverance is the greatest of gains". We take it to mean that merely getting away alive is the best he can hope for, but the wording is odd and the text may be damaged. بِطْرِيق is the Byzantine title "patrician" (Greek patrikios); the bi- is part of the word. The sentence is an unreal condition: لَوْ with the past, and لَـ opening the answer.

sentences.t: فَقُلْ لَنَا مَا الَّذِي تُرِيدُ فَإِنْ أَرَدْتَ أَنْ نَهْدِيَكَ إِلَى الطَّرِيقِ هَدَيْنَاكَ وَإِنْ أَرَدْتَ الرِّفْدَ أَرْفَدْنَاكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qul lanā mā alladhī turīdu fa-in aradta an nahdiyaka ilā al-ṭarīqi hadaynāka wa-in aradta al-rifda arfadnāka
sentences.l: So say to us what is that which you want. And if you want that we guide you to the road, we guided you; and if you want the gift, we gifted you.
sentences.i: So tell us what you want. If you wish us to set you on the road, we will set you on it; and if you wish for a gift, we will give you one.
sentences.n: هَدَيْنَاكَ and أَرْفَدْنَاكَ are past tenses with the force of a promise, "we have guided you, i.e. we will": the result of the condition is stated as already done. نَهْدِيَكَ is subjunctive after أَنْ; هَدَى takes the direct object plus إِلَى. الرِّفْد is a gift or help given to someone.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ شَرْكَانُ كَلَامَهَا قَالَ لَهَا أَنَارَجُلٌ غَرِيبٌ مِنَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَقَدْ سِرْتُ فِي هَذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ مُنْفَرِدًا بِنَفْسِي أَطْلُبُ الْغَنِيمَةَ فَلَمْ أَجِلْ غَنِيمَةً أَحْسَنَ مِنْ هَؤُلَاءِ الْجَوَارِى الْعَشْرَةِ فِي هَذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ الْمُقْمِرَةِ فَآخُذُهُنَّ وَأَلْحَقُ بِهِنَّ إِلَى أَصْحَابِي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa Sharkānu kalāmahā qāla lahā anā rajulun gharībun mina al-muslimīna wa-qad sirtu fī hādhihi al-laylati munfaridan bi-nafsī aṭlubu al-ghanīmata fa-lam ajil ghanīmatan aḥsana min hāʾulāʾi al-jawārī al-ʿashrati fī hādhihi al-laylati al-muqmirati fa-ākhuduhunna wa-alḥaqu bihinna ilā aṣḥābī
sentences.l: And when Sharkān heard her speech, he said to her: I am a man, a stranger, of the Muslims, and I journeyed in this night alone by myself, seeking booty; and I did not find a booty finer than these ten slave-girls in this moonlit night; so I take them and go along with them to my companions.
sentences.i: When Sharkān had heard her words he said to her: I am a stranger, a man of the Muslims. I rode out alone tonight in search of spoil, and I have found none finer than these ten girls on this moonlit night; so I mean to take them and carry them along with me to my companions.
sentences.n: أَنَارَجُلٌ is printed as one word, anā + rajul. فَلَمْ أَجِلْ is printed with a lām where sense wants a dāl: the word is surely a misprint for أَجِدْ ("I did not find"). We point the letters as printed (ajil) but translate the intended "find". The edition prints الْجَوَارِى with ى and here the plural stands in apposition to "these". The last two verbs, آخُذُهُنَّ and أَلْحَقُ بِهِنَّ, are given as plain imperfects, "I take them and go along with them"; لَحِقَ بِـ is "to join, go along with". Notice that Sharkān begins his answer by speaking as an unknown stranger, not as the prince that he is.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ الْجَارِيَةُ اعْلَمْ أَنَّ الْغَنِيمَةَ مَا وَصَلْتَ إِلَيْهَا وَالْجَوَارِي وَاللَّهِ مَا هُنَّ غَنِيمَتُكَ أَمَا قُلْتُ لَكَ أَنَّ الْكَذِبَ شَيْنٌ فَقَالَ لَهَا الْعَاقِلُ مَنْ يَعْتَبِرُ بِغَيْرِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu al-jāriyatu iʿlam anna al-ghanīmata mā waṣalta ilayhā wa-al-jawārī wa-Allāhi mā hunna ghanīmatuka a-mā qultu laka anna al-kadhiba shaynun fa-qāla lahā al-ʿāqilu man yaʿtabiru bi-ghayrihi
sentences.l: And the girl said to him: Know that the booty — you have not reached it; and the slave-girls, by God, they are not your booty. Did I not say to you that lying is a blemish? He said to her: The wise one is he who takes warning by another.
sentences.i: The girl said to him: Know that you have not come near that spoil, and as for these girls, by God, they are not your prize. Did I not tell you that lying is a disgrace? He said to her: The wise man is he who takes warning from another.
sentences.n: The girl has seen through his boast, and says so; the unit is her answer and his reply. اَلْعَاقِلُ مَنْ يَعْتَبِرُ بِغَيْرِهِ is a proverb: "the wise is he who learns from someone else's example". اعْتَبَرَ takes بِـ for the thing from which a lesson is drawn. Sharkān is turning her "truth" speech back on her: she has said that lying is shameful, and he answers that a clever man learns from what has happened to others, that is, he will not try the sword again.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ وَحَقِّ الْمَسِيحِ لَوْلَا أَخَافُ أَنْ يَكُونَ هَلَاكُكَ عَلَى يَدِي لَكُنْتُ صِحْتُ صَيْحَةً مَلَأَتْ عَلَيْكَ الْمَرْجَ خَيْلًا وَرِجَالًا وَلَكِنْ أَنَا أُشْفِقُ عَلَى الْغَرِيبِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu wa-ḥaqqi al-Masīḥi law-lā akhāfu an yakūna halākuka ʿalā yadī la-kuntu ṣiḥtu ṣayḥatan malaʾat ʿalayka al-marja khaylan wa-rijālan wa-lākin anā ushfiqu ʿalā al-gharībi
sentences.l: And she said to him: By the right of the Messiah, were it not that I fear that your destruction be at my hand, I would have cried a cry that would fill the meadow upon you with horses and men; but I, I take pity on the stranger.
sentences.i: She said to him: By the Messiah's right, were I not afraid that your death would come at my hands, I would have let out such a cry as would fill the meadow around you with horse and foot. But I take pity on a stranger.
sentences.n: وَحَقِّ الْمَسِيحِ, "by the right of the Messiah", shows the girl is a Christian, one of the Byzantine girls. لَوْلَا أَخَافُ puts a verb after لَوْلَا, which in Classical takes a noun; we read it as "if I were not afraid", and note it as Middle Arabic. لَكُنْتُ صِحْتُ, kāna plus the past, is "I would have shouted". خَيْلًا وَرِجَالًا, "horses and men", is a common pair for cavalry and infantry.

sentences.t: وَإِنْ أَرَدْتَ الْغَنِيمَةَ فَأَنَا أَطْلُبُ مِنْكَ أَنْ تَنْزِلَ عَنْ جَوَادِكَ وَتَحْلِفَ لِي بِدِينِكَ أَنَّكَ لَاتَتَقَرَّبُ إِلَيَّ بِشَيُ مِنَ السِّلَاحِ وَأَتَصَارَعَ أَنَا وَإِيَّاكَ فَإِنْ صَرَعْتَنِي فَضَعْنِي عَلَى جَوَادِكَ وَخُذْنَا كُلَّنَا غَنِيمَةً
sentences.tr: wa-in aradta al-ghanīmata fa-anā aṭlubu minka an tanzila ʿan jawādika wa-taḥlifa lī bi-dīnika annaka lā tataqarrabu ilayya bi-shayu mina al-silāḥi wa-ataṣāraʿa anā wa-iyyāka fa-in ṣaraʿtanī fa-ḍaʿnī ʿalā jawādika wa-khudhnā kullanā ghanīmatan
sentences.l: And if you want the booty, then I ask of you that you dismount from your steed and swear to me by your religion that you will not draw near to me with anything of weapons, and that I wrestle, I and you; so if you throw me, then put me upon your steed and take us, all of us, as booty;
sentences.i: And if it is spoil you want, then I ask you to dismount from your horse and swear to me by your faith that you will come at me with no weapon of any kind, and that you and I shall wrestle. If you throw me, set me on your horse and take us all as your spoil;
sentences.n: لَاتَتَقَرَّبُ is printed as one word. In بِشَيُ the edition itself puts a damma on the yā: it stands for بِشَيْءٍ, "with anything", and we keep the printed mark as it is and read shayʾ. وَإِيَّاكَ, "and you", uses the object form of the pronoun as the partner in the wrestling (Classical would say وَأَنْتَ); this is common in Middle Arabic. The three verbs after أَنْ, تَنْزِلَ, تَحْلِفَ, أَتَصَارَعَ, all depend on the one أَنْ.

sentences.t: وَإِنْ أَنَا صَرَعْتُكَ أَتَحَكَّمُ فِيكَ فَاحْلِفْ لِي عَلَى ذَلِكَ فَإِنِّي أَخَافُ مِنْ غَدْرِكَ فَقَدْ وَرَدَ فِى الْأَخْبَارِ إِذَا كَانَ الْغَدْرُ طِبَاعًا فَإِنَّ الثِّقَةَ بِكُلِّ أَحَدٍ عَجْزٌ فَإِنْ حَلَفْتَ لِي عَدَيْتُ إِلَيْكَ وَأَتَيْتُكَ وَجِئْتُ عِنْدَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-in anā ṣaraʿtuka ataḥakkamu fīka fa-iḥlif lī ʿalā dhālika fa-innī akhāfu min ghadrika fa-qad warada fī al-akhbāri idhā kāna al-ghadru ṭibāʿan fa-inna al-thiqata bi-kulli aḥadin ʿajzun fa-in ḥalafta lī ʿadaytu ilayka wa-ataytuka wa-jiʾtu ʿindaka
sentences.l: and if I throw you, I exercise judgement over you. So swear to me upon that, for I fear from your treachery — for it is reported in the reports: If treachery is a nature, then trust in anyone is incapacity. So if you swear to me, I will cross over to you and come to you and come to your side.
sentences.i: but if I throw you, I shall do with you as I please. So swear to me on this, for I fear treachery from you; it is told in the old sayings that if treachery is a man's nature, then to trust anyone at all is folly. If you swear to me, I will cross over to you and come to you, to your side.
sentences.n: The unit continues the girl's long speech. أَتَحَكَّمُ فِيكَ, "I will have my way with you", answers the condition in the plain imperfect; Classical would use the jussive. إِذَا كَانَ الْغَدْرُ طِبَاعًا فَإِنَّ الثِّقَةَ بِكُلِّ أَحَدٍ عَجْزٌ is quoted as a saying from "the reports" (الْأَخْبَار): treachery is a man's nature, so to trust everyone is weakness. عَدَيْتُ إِلَيْكَ, "I crossed over to you", is again a past tense standing for a promise. جِئْتُ عِنْدَكَ uses ʿinda, where Classical wants إِلَى; it means "I came to your side".

sentences.t: فَقَالَ شَرْكَانُ وَقَدْ طَمِعَ فِي أَخْذِهَا وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ إِنَّهَا لَمْ تَعْرِفْ أَنِّي بَطَلٌ مِنَ الْأَبْطَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Sharkānu wa-qad ṭamiʿa fī akhdhihā wa-qāla fī nafsihi innahā lam taʿrif annī baṭalun mina abṭāl
sentences.l: And Sharkān said — and he had coveted the taking of her — and said in himself: Indeed she did not know that I am a hero of the heroes;
sentences.i: Now Sharkān, who had begun to covet taking her, said to himself: She does not know that I am one of the great champions.
sentences.n: فَقَالَ شَرْكَانُ … وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ has two qāla verbs in a row, the first left without its speech: the sentence is run together in the print, and the thing he says is his thought. The circumstantial clause وَقَدْ طَمِعَ فِي أَخْذِهَا says he had already set his heart on capturing her. بَطَلٌ مِنَ الْأَبْطَالِ is "a hero among heroes", a champion of the first rank.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَادَاهَا وَقَالَ لَهَا حَلِّفِينِي بِمَا أَرَدْتِ وَبِمَا تَثِقِينَ بِهِ أَنِّي لَا أَقْرَبُكِ بِشَيٌ حَتَّى تَأْخُذِي أُهْبَتَكِ وَتَقُولِي ادْنُ مِنِّي لِأُصَارِعَكِ فَحِينَئِذٍ أَتَقَرَّبُ إِلَيْكِ فَإِنْ صَرَعْتِنِي فَإِنَّ لِي مِنَ الْمَالِ مَا أَشْتَرِي بِهِ نَفْسِي وَإِنْ صَرَعْتُكِ أَنَا فَهِيَ الْغَنِيمَةُ الْكُبْرَى
sentences.tr: thumma nādāhā wa-qāla lahā ḥallifīnī bi-mā aradti wa-bi-mā tathiqīna bihi annī lā aqrabuki bi-shayun ḥattā taʾkhudhī uhbataki wa-taqūlī udnu minnī li-uṣāriʿaka fa-ḥīnaʾidhin ataqarrabu ilayki fa-in ṣaraʿtinī fa-inna lī mina al-māli mā ashtarī bihi nafsī wa-in ṣaraʿtuki anā fa-hiya al-ghanīmatu al-kubrā
sentences.l: Then he called to her and said to her: Make me swear by what you want and by what you trust in, that I will not approach you with anything until you take your gear and say: Draw near to me that I may wrestle you; and at that time I will draw near to you. So if you throw me, then I have of wealth what I buy myself with; and if I throw you, it is the greatest booty.
sentences.i: Then he called to her and said: Make me swear by whatever you wish and by whatever you trust, that I will not come near you with anything until you have taken up your gear and said, "Come to me, that I may wrestle you"; only then will I approach you. If you throw me, I have money enough to buy myself free; and if I throw you, then you are the greatest prize of all.
sentences.n: The edition prints حَلِّفيني with a fatḥa on the ḥā and a kasra-and-shadda on the lām; those marks are kept, and the rest is added: ḥallifīnī, "make me swear" (imperative, feminine, since he speaks to the girl). Here again, بِشَيٌ is printed with a tanwīn on the yā, for شَيْء. أُهْبَتَكِ is "your readiness", that is, until she has put herself in order for the contest. Sharkān's last word, الْغَنِيمَةُ الْكُبْرَى, is the "greatest booty", and the pronoun فَهِيَ can be read as the girl herself or the whole of the spoil.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ أَنَا رَضِيتُ بِذَلِكَ فَتَحَيَّرَ شَرْكَانُ فِي ذَلِكَ وَقَالَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-jāriyatu anā raḍītu bi-dhālika fa-taḥayyara Sharkānu fī dhālika qāla
sentences.l: And the girl said: I am content with that. And Sharkān was bewildered at that, and said —
sentences.i: The girl said: I am content with that. At this Sharkān was bewildered, and said —
sentences.n: Sharkān is bewildered presumably because she accepts so readily. The unit ends with وَقَالَ; what he says is the next unit.

sentences.t: وَحَقِّ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ رَضِيتُ أَنَا الْآخَرُ
sentences.tr: wa-ḥaqqi al-nabiyyi ṣallā Allāhu ʿalayhi wa-sallama raḍītu anā al-ākhar
sentences.l: And by the right of the Prophet — God bless him and give him peace — I was content, I, the other.
sentences.i: By the Prophet's right, God bless him and give him peace, I am content as well.
sentences.n: Sharkān speaks. Bewildered that the girl accepts his terms so readily, he swears by the Prophet that he too is content. الْآخَرُ, "the other", stands in apposition to أَنَا, so the clause means "I too, for my part, am content". The formula صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ is the blessing spoken after the Prophet's name.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ احْلِفِ الْآنَ بِمَنْ رَكَّبَ الْأَرْوَاحَ فِى الْأَشْبَاحِ وَشَرَعَ الشَّرَائِعَ لِلْأَنَامِ إِنَّكَ لَوْتَتَعَرَّضُ لِي بِسُوءٍ غَيْرَ الْمُصَارَعَةِ تَمُوتُ عَلَى غَيْرِدِينِ الْإِسْلَامِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu iḥlifi al-āna bi-man rakkaba al-arwāḥa fī al-ashbāḥi wa-sharaʿa al-sharāʾiʿa li-al-anāmi innaka law tataʿarraḍu lī bi-sūʾin ghayra al-muṣāraʿati tamūtu ʿalā ghayri dīni al-islām
sentences.l: So she said to him: Swear now by Him who put-together the spirits in the bodies and laid-down the laws for the people: that you, if you expose yourself to me with evil other-than the wrestling, die upon other-than the religion of Islam.
sentences.i: Then she said to him: Swear now, by Him who set the spirits in their bodies and gave laws to mankind, that if you offer me any harm beyond the wrestling, you die outside the faith of Islam.
sentences.n: Two pairs of words are printed run together and kept so: لَوْتَتَعَرَّضُ (law + tataʿarraḍu) and غَيْرِدِينِ (ghayri + dīni). The oath asks Sharkān to stake his religion on keeping to the wrestling only. تَعَرَّضَ لِـ means "to make an attempt upon, to offer an affront to", and بِسُوءٍ gives the means of it, "with evil". The ending of both oath-clauses, in -āḥ / -ām, is a little sajʿ.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ شَرْكَانُ وَاللَّهِ لَوْحَلَّفَنِي قَاضٍ وَلَوْكَانَ قَاضِى الْقُضَاةِ لَمْ يُحَلِّفْنِي بِهَذِهِ الْأَيْمَانِ ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ حَلَفَ لَهَا بِجَمِيعِ مَا ذَكَرَتْهُ وَرَبَطَ جَوَادَهُ فِى الْأَشْجَارِ وَهُوَ غَرِيقٌ فِي بَحْرِالِافْتِكَارِ وَقَالَ سُبْحَانَ مَنْ صَوَّرَهَا مِنْ مَاءٍ مَهِينٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Sharkānu wa-Allāhi law ḥallafanī qāḍin wa-law kāna qāḍī al-quḍāti lam yuḥallifnī bi-hādhihi al-aymāni thumma innahu ḥalafa lahā bi-jamīʿi mā dhakaratuhu wa-rabaṭa jawādahu fī al-ashjāri wa-huwa gharīqun fī baḥri al-iftikāri wa-qāla subḥāna man ṣawwarahā min māʾin mahīn
sentences.l: So Sharkān said: By God, if a judge had made me swear — and were he the judge of the judges — he would not have made me swear by these oaths. Then he swore to her by all that she had mentioned, and tethered his steed among the trees, while he was a drowned-one in the sea of the pondering, and said: Glory to Him who fashioned her from lowly water.
sentences.i: Sharkān said: By God, if a judge were to put me on oath — were he the chief judge himself — he would not lay such oaths upon me. Yet he swore to her by everything she had named, and tethered his horse among the trees, drowning in a sea of thought, and said: Glory to Him who shaped her out of lowly water!
sentences.n: لَوْحَلَّفَنِي and وَلَوْكَانَ are printed with لَوْ attached to the next word; the edition does this often, and we keep it. After لَمْ the verb is jussive, hence لَمْ يُحَلِّفْنِي with a sukūn before the object-ending -nī. مَاءٍ مَهِينٍ, "lowly water", is a Qurʾānic phrase (for example 32:8) for the humble fluid from which humankind is made; here it is Sharkān's cry of wonder that so lovely a form came from so humble a source. بَحْرِالِافْتِكَارِ is printed as one word, "the sea of reflection"; the kasra on the lām is the usual pointing of a word like الِافْتِكَار whose second alif is a connecting alif.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ شَرْكَانَ اشْتَدَّ وَأَخَذَ أُهْبَتَهُ لِلصِّرَاعِ وَقَالَ لِلْجَارِيَةِ عَلَى النَّهْرِ وَاعْبُرِي فَقَالَتْ لَهُ لَيْسَ لِي إِلَيْكَ عُبُورٌ فَإِنْ كُنْتَ تُرِيدُ فَاعْبُرْأَنْتَ إِلَى عِنْدِي
sentences.tr: thumma inna Sharkāna ishtadda wa-akhadha uhbatahu li-al-ṣirāʿi wa-qāla li-al-jāriyati ʿalā al-nahri wa-iʿburī fa-qālat lahu laysa lī ilayka ʿubūrun fa-in kunta turīdu fa-iʿbur anta ilā ʿindī
sentences.l: Then indeed Sharkān braced himself and took his equipment for the wrestling, and said to the girl, on the river: And cross! So she said to him: There is not for me to you a crossing; so if you wish, cross, you, to at-me.
sentences.i: Then Sharkān braced himself, made ready for the wrestling, and called to the girl across the river, "Come over!" But she said to him, "I have no way over to you. If you wish it, cross yourself to me."
sentences.n: عَلَى النَّهْرِ says where the girl stood, on the far side of the stream, and the command وَاعْبُرِي is feminine, addressed to her. فَاعْبُرْأَنْتَ is printed as one word: the imperative with the pronoun أَنْتَ added for emphasis, "you cross." إِلَى عِنْدِي stacks two prepositions, literally "to at-me", for "to where I am"; Classical Arabic would say إِلَيَّ, so you can mark it as a colloquial turn.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا شَرْكَانُ أَتَا لَا أَقْدِرُ عَلَى ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā Sharkānu atā lā aqdiru ʿalā dhālik
sentences.l: So Sharkān said to her: Atā — I am not able upon that.
sentences.i: Sharkān said to her, "I cannot do that."
sentences.n: The edition prints أتا here; it is a slip for أَنَا, "I". The letters are kept as printed and pointed أَتَا, but read it as anā. The sense is plain: he cannot cross the river.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ يَافَتَى أَنَا أَجِي لَكَ ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا شَمَّرَتْ أَذْ يَا لَهَا وَقَفَزَتْ فَصَارَتْ عِنْدَهُ فِى الْجَانِبِ الْآخَرِ مِنَ النَّهْرِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-jāriyatu yā fatā anā ajī laka thumma innahā shammarat adh yā lahā wa-qafazat fa-ṣārat ʿindahu fī al-jānibi al-ākhari mina al-nahr
sentences.l: So the girl said: O youth, I come to you. Then indeed she tucked-up — adh yā lahā — and leapt, and became at him on the other side of the river.
sentences.i: The girl said, "Young man, I will come to you." Then she gathered up her skirts, sprang across, and landed beside him on the near bank.
sentences.n: اذ يا لها is a wrongly divided أَذْيَالَهَا, "her skirts" (the pieces of the print are pointed as printed). شَمَّرَ is "to tuck up" a robe for action. أَجِي, "I come", is the colloquial verb for Classical آتِي (and the sense is "I will come"); it is the first Middle Arabic form of the passage. يَافَتَى is printed as one word. فِى الْجَانِبِ الْآخَرِ is, strictly, the other side from the one she left, so the same side as Sharkān.

sentences.t: فَدَنَا مِنْهَا وَ انْحَنٰي وَصَفَّقَ بِيَدَيْهِ وَهُوَ بَاهِتٌ فِي حُسْنِهَا وَجَمَالِهَا فَرَأَى صُورَةً قَدِ اغْتَرَفَتْهَا يَدُ الْقُدْرَةِ بِوَرَقَةِ الْجَانِ وَرَبَّتْهَا يَدُ الْعِنَايَةِ وَهَبَّتْ عَلَيْهَا نَسَمَاتُ السُّعُودِ وَقَابَلَهَا عِنْدَ خِلْقَتِهَا طَالِعٌ مَسْعُودٌ
sentences.tr: fa-danā minhā wa-inḥanā wa-ṣaffaqa bi-yadayhi wa-huwa bāhitun fī ḥusnihā wa-jamālihā fa-raʾā ṣūratan qadi ightarafathā yadu al-qudrati bi-waraqati al-jāni wa-rabbathā yadu al-ʿināyati wa-habbat ʿalayhā nasamātu al-suʿūdi wa-qābalahā ʿinda khilqatihā ṭāliʿun masʿūd
sentences.l: So he drew near from her, and he bent, and clapped with his two hands, he being dazed in her beauty and her loveliness; and he saw a form that the hand of Power had scooped-up with the leaf of the Jān, and the hand of Providence had reared, and the breezes of felicities had blown upon, and a felicitous ascendant had met at her creating.
sentences.i: He drew near her, and stooped, and clapped his hands, dazed by her beauty and her grace; for he saw a form that the hand of Power had scooped up with a leaf of paradise, that the hand of Providence had nursed, that the soft airs of good fortune had breathed upon, and that a lucky star had met at its making.
sentences.n: The print breaks the line after the conjunction وَ and the next line begins with انحني; we keep them as two words. انحني is the print's spelling of انحنى, so it is pointed with a dagger alif over the yā to read inḥanā. The hand-clap is both amazement and the wrestlers' challenge, which she answers in the next unit but one. In بِوَرَقَةِ الْجَانِ the last word is printed الجان and pointed as printed, al-jān ("the jinn"); the phrase is obscure, and it may be a slip for الجنان, "the gardens (of paradise)", which is the sense the idiomatic line follows. Note the sajʿ at the end: السُّعُودِ / مَسْعُودٌ. طَالِعٌ is the ascendant, the star-sign rising at one's birth or making.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْجَارِيَةَ أَتَتْ وَنَادَتْهُ يَا مُسْلِمُ تَقَدَّمْ إِلَى الصِّرَاعِ قَبْلَ أَنْ يَطْلُعَ الْفَجْرُ وَشَمَّرَتْ عَنْ سَاعِدٍ دَنُّهُ الْجُبْنِّ الطَّرِيِّ فَأَضَاءَ ذَلِكَ الْمَكَانُ مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-jāriyata atat wa-nādathu yā muslimu taqaddam ilā al-ṣirāʿi qabla an yaṭluʿa al-fajru wa-shammarat ʿan sāʿidin dannuhu al-jubnni al-ṭariyyi fa-aḍāʾa dhālika al-makānu minhu
sentences.l: Then indeed the girl came and called him: O Muslim, step forward to the wrestling before the dawn rises! And she tucked-up from a forearm — dannuhu — the fresh cheese, so that place was lit from it.
sentences.i: Then the girl came and called to him, "Muslim, step forward to the wrestling before the dawn comes up!" And she bared a forearm like fresh curd, so that the whole place was lit by it.
sentences.n: دنه is obscure, and the print may be corrupt: we point it dannuhu as printed, and the translation assumes it stands for كَأَنَّهُ, "as if it were". The print also puts a shadda on the final nūn of الجبنّ, which we keep over a kasra; it is the edition's own mark and is not explained. Pale, soft, fresh cheese is a compliment to the whiteness of the arm. She calls him يَا مُسْلِمُ, "Muslim", as the Christian addressing the Muslim prince, who has not named himself. فَأَضَاءَ is the intransitive verb, "shone": the place lit up by the arm's brightness.

sentences.t: هَذَا وَشَرْكَانُ قَدْ تَحَيَّرَ وَانْحَنَى وَصَفَّقَ بِيَدَيْهِ وَصَفَّقَتِ الْأُخْرَى بِيَدَيْهَا وَتَعَلَّقَتْ بِهِ وَتَعَلَّقَ بِهَا وَتَعَانَقَا وَتَمَاسَكَا وَتَعَارَكَا
sentences.tr: hādhā wa-Sharkānu qad taḥayyara wa-inḥanā wa-ṣaffaqa bi-yadayhi wa-ṣaffaqati al-ukhrā bi-yadayhā wa-taʿallaqat bihi wa-taʿallaqa bihā wa-taʿānaqā wa-tamāsakā wa-taʿārakā
sentences.l: This — and Sharkān had been bewildered — and he bent, and clapped with his two hands, and the other clapped with her two hands, and she clung to him and he clung to her, and they embraced, and gripped one another, and grappled.
sentences.i: Meanwhile Sharkān, bewildered, stooped and clapped his hands, and the other clapped hers; then she took hold of him and he of her, and they embraced and gripped and grappled.
sentences.n: هَذَا at the head of a sentence is the narrator's "meanwhile", turning from her to Sharkān. الْأُخْرَى, "the other", is the girl: the narrator keeps her unnamed. The last three verbs are all Form VI, the pattern for an action done to each other, so they are dual: "they embraced one another", and so on.

sentences.t: فَوَضَعَ يَدَهُ عَلَى خَصْرِهَا النَّحِيلِ فَغَاصَتْ أَنَا مِلُهُ فِي طَبَقَاتِ بَطْنِهَا وَاسْتَرْخَتْ أَعْضَاؤُهُ فَوَقَفَ عَلَى مَقَامِ الْحَسْرَةِ فَبَانَ لَهُ بَطْنٌ فِيهِ الْفَتْرَةُ وَصَارَ يَرْتَعِدُ مِثْلَ الْقَصَبَةِ الْفَارِسِيَّةِ فِى الرِّيحِ الْعَاصِفِ فَرَفَعَتْهُ وَضَرَبَتْ بِالْأَرْضِ وَجَلَسَتْ عَلَى صَدْرِهِ بِكَفَلٍ كَأَنَّهُ كَثِيبُ رَمْلٍ فَلَمْ يَمْلِكْ نَفْسَهُ عَقْلًا
sentences.tr: fa-waḍaʿa yadahu ʿalā khaṣrihā al-naḥīli fa-ghāṣat anā miluhu fī ṭabaqāti baṭnihā wa-istarkhat aʿḍāʾuhu fa-waqafa ʿalā maqāmi al-ḥasrati fa-bāna lahu baṭnun fīhi al-fatratu wa-ṣāra yartaʿidu mithla al-qaṣabati al-fārisiyyati fī al-rīḥi al-ʿāṣifi fa-rafaʿathu wa-ḍarabat bi-al-arḍi wa-jalasat ʿalā ṣadrihi bi-kafalin kaʾannahu kathību ramlin fa-lam yamlik nafsahu ʿaqlan
sentences.l: So he put his hand on her slender waist, and his fingertips sank into the layers of her belly, and his limbs went slack, and he halted at the station of regret; and there showed itself to him a belly in which was the languor, and he began to shake like the Persian reed in the raging wind. Then she lifted him and struck against the ground, and sat on his chest with a rump as though it were a dune of sand, and he did not control himself, in mind.
sentences.i: He laid his hand on her slender waist, and his fingertips sank into the folds of her belly; his limbs went slack, and he stood still in a place of dismay. A belly showed itself to him in which lay languor, and he began to shake like a Persian reed in a raging wind. Then she lifted him and dashed him to the ground, and sat on his chest on haunches like a sand-dune, and he could not command his own wits.
sentences.n: أَنَا مِلُهُ is a wrongly divided أَنَامِلُهُ, "his fingertips"; the pieces are pointed as printed. In أَعْضَاؤُهُ the print spells the hamza seat as a plain waw. The clause فَبَانَ لَهُ بَطْنٌ فِيهِ الْفَتْرَةُ is hard to be sure of: the likeliest sense is that her soft belly drained his strength (فَتْرَة, "slackness, languor"), but the grammar leaves it open whose belly is meant. وَضَرَبَتْ بِالْأَرْضِ has no object in the print: it stands for ضَرَبَتْ بِهِ الْأَرْضَ, "she dashed him on the ground". كَثِيبُ رَمْلٍ is a heap of sand, a dune. عَقْلًا is an accusative of respect, "as to wits", so "he lost control of himself in mind". The print's كأنه carries its own hamza on the alif.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ يَا مُسْلِمُ أَنْتُمْ عِنْدَكُمْ قَتْلُ النَّصَارَى مُبَاحٌ فَمَا قَوْلُكَ فِي قَتْلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu yā muslimu antum ʿindakum qatlu al-naṣārā mubāḥun fa-mā qawluka fī qatlik
sentences.l: So she said to him: O Muslim, you — with you the killing of the Christians is permitted; so what is your saying about your killing?
sentences.i: She said to him, "Muslim, with you the killing of Christians is lawful; so what do you say to your own killing?"
sentences.n: أَنْتُمْ عِنْدَكُمْ … is a fronted topic, "as for you, with you …"; مُبَاحٌ is the legal term for "permitted". قَتْلِكَ is the killing of you, that is, your being killed, not your killing of anyone.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا يَا سَيِّدَتِي أَمَّا قَوْلُكِ عَنْ قَتْلِي فَمَا هُوَ إِلَّاحَرَامٌ فَإِنَّ نَبِيَّنَا مُحَمَّدًا صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ نَهَى عَنْ قَتْلِ النِّسْوَانِ وَالصِّبْيَانِ وَالشُّيُوخِ وَالرُّهْبَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā yā sayyidatī ammā qawluki ʿan qatlī fa-mā huwa illā ḥarāmun fa-inna nabiyyanā Muḥammadan ṣallā Allāhu ʿalayhi wa-sallama nahā ʿan qatli al-niswāni wa-al-ṣibyāni wa-al-shuyūkhi wa-al-ruhbān
sentences.l: So he said to her: O my lady, as for your saying about my killing, it is not but forbidden; for our Prophet Muḥammad — God bless him and give him peace — forbade the killing of the womenfolk and the boys and the elders and the monks.
sentences.i: He answered, "My lady, as for what you say of killing me, it is nothing but forbidden; for our Prophet Muḥammad, God bless him and give him peace, forbade the slaying of women, children, old men and monks."
sentences.n: The print runs إِلَّا and حَرَام together as الاحرام, "except forbidden"; we keep it as one word. Sharkān argues from the rule that protects non-combatants (women, children, the aged, monks). The joke is that he claims their immunity for himself, a strong young prince who has just been thrown. سَيِّدَتِي, "my lady", is the polite address to a woman; note that he has become suddenly courteous.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ إِذَا كَانَ نَبِيُّكُمْ أُوحِيَ إِلَيْهِ بِهَذَا فَيَنْبَغِي أَنْ نُكَافِئَهُ عَلَى ذَلِكَ وَلَكِنْ قَدْ وَهَبْتُكَ نَفْسَكَ فَمَا يَضِيعُ عِنْدَ الْإِنْسَانِ الْإِحْسَانُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu idhā kāna nabiyyukum ūḥiya ilayhi bi-hādhā fa-yanbaghī an nukāfiʾahu ʿalā dhālika wa-lākin qad wahabtuka nafsaka fa-mā yaḍīʿu ʿinda al-insāni al-iḥsān
sentences.l: So she said to him: If your prophet was inspired-to with this, then it is fitting that we requite him for that; but I have given you your self, for the benefaction is not lost with the human.
sentences.i: She said to him, "If this was revealed to your prophet, it is only right that we repay him for it. So I give you back your own life, for kindness is never wasted on a human being."
sentences.n: اوحي is printed with a final yā; that is the print's spelling, and we point it as the passive أُوحِيَ, "was revealed", with أُوحِيَ إِلَيْهِ the standard phrase for prophetic revelation. وَهَبْتُكَ نَفْسَكَ, "I have given you your self", is the idiom for granting someone his life. The closing clause is a maxim: kindness shown to a person is not lost. She wins the argument by taking his own prophet's rule as law, so he is spared.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَامَتْ عَنْ صَدْرِ شَرْكَانَ وَقَامَ يَنْفُضُ التُّرَابَ عَنْ رَأْسِهِ مِنْ ذَوَاتِ الضِّلَعِ الْأَعْوَجِ وَمَا هِيَ الْأَمَانَتْ
sentences.tr: thumma qāmat ʿan ṣadri Sharkāna wa-qāma yanfuḍu al-turāba ʿan raʾsihi min dhawāti al-ḍilaʿi al-aʿwaji wa-mā hiya al-amānat
sentences.l: Then she rose from the chest of Sharkān, and he rose shaking the dust from his head, from the possessors-of the rib, the crooked; and what is she, the trust?
sentences.i: Then she rose from Sharkān's chest, and he got to his feet brushing the dust from his head, beaten by one of the crooked-ribbed sex; and what manner of trust is she?
sentences.n: عَنْ صَدْرِ شَرْكَانَ is "off Sharkān's chest". ذَوَاتُ الضِّلَعِ الْأَعْوَجِ, "those of the crooked rib", is a stock jibe at women, from the saying that woman was made from a crooked rib; Sharkān is smarting at being thrown by one. وَمَا هِيَ الْأَمَانَتْ is obscure. The print has تْ where the usual spelling is ة (a Middle Arabic form), and I read it as "and what is she, the trust?", perhaps a sneer that such a woman is no trustworthy deposit. It may also be corrupt, so hold the reading loosely.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لَهُ لَا تَخْجَلْ فَمَنْ يَدْخُلُ بِلَادَ الرُّومِ يُرِيدُ الْغَنِيمَةَ وَيُعِينُ الْمُلُوكَ عَلَى الْمُلُوكِ كَيْفَ لَا يَكُونُ فِيهِ قُوَّةٌ حَتَّى لَا يَقْدِرُ يُدَافِعُ عَنْ نَفْسِهِ ذَاتُ الضِّلَعِ الْأَعْوَجِ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat lahu lā takhjal fa-man yadkhulu bilāda al-Rūmi yurīdu al-ghanīmata wa-yuʿīnu al-mulūka ʿalā al-mulūki kayfa lā yakūnu fīhi quwwatun ḥattā lā yaqdiru yudāfiʿu ʿan nafsihi dhātu al-ḍilaʿi al-aʿwaj
sentences.l: And she said to him: Do not be ashamed; for whoever enters the lands of Rūm, wanting the booty and helping kings against kings — how is there not strength in him, until he cannot defend about himself? — she of the crooked rib.
sentences.i: And she said to him: Do not be ashamed. A man who enters the land of Rūm in quest of spoil, and lends his aid to kings against kings — how should he lack strength, so that he could not defend himself? — so said she of the crooked rib.
sentences.n: ذَاتُ الضِّلَعِ الْأَعْوَجِ closes her speech with no connecting word. It repeats the jibe of the previous unit, and I take it as a tag naming the speaker; the syntax gives no firm hold, so treat the reading as uncertain. حَتَّى لَا يَقْدِرُ يُدَافِعُ puts two imperfects side by side with no أَنْ, which is Middle Arabic. Her argument is that a man bold enough to invade Rūm for loot must be strong, so there is no disgrace in his fall.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا مَاهِيَ لِضَعْفِ قُوَّتِي وَلَا صَرَعْتِنِي بِقُوَّتِكِ وَلَكِنْ جَمَالُكِ هُوَ الَّذِي صَرَعَنِي فَإِنْ أَنْعَمْتِ إِلَيَّ بِدَسْتٍ آخَرَ كَانَ مِنْ نَوَالِكِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā māhiya li-ḍaʿfi quwwatī wa-lā ṣaraʿtinī bi-quwwatiki wa-lākin jamāluki huwa alladhī ṣaraʿanī fa-in anʿamti ilayya bi-dastin ākhara kāna min nawāliki
sentences.l: So he said to her: It is not for weakness of my strength, and you did not throw me by your strength, but your beauty it is that threw me; so if you would show-grace to me with another bout, it would be of your bounty.
sentences.i: He said to her: It was not weakness of strength that undid me, nor did your strength throw me; it was your beauty that threw me. If you would grant me another bout, it would be of your bounty.
sentences.n: ماهي is printed as one word, "it is not"; the لِـ after it means "because of". دَسْت is Persian dast, "hand", used here for a round or bout of a contest; it returns below. أَنْعَمَ إِلَى بِـ is "to favour someone with something", and the بِـ marks the favour granted.

sentences.t: فَضَحِكَتْ وَقَالَتْ أَجَبْتُكَ إِلَى ذَلِكَ غَيْرَأَنَّ الْجَوَارِيَ طَالَ بِهِمُ الْكِتَافُ وَقَدْ كَلَّتْ مِنْهُمُ السَّوَاعِدُ وَالْأَطْرَافُ وَالصَّوَابُ أَنِّي أَحُلُّهُمْ فَلَرُبَّمَا طَالَ الصِّرَاعُ فِي هَذَا الدَّسْتِ مَعَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-ḍaḥikat wa-qālat ajabtuka ilā dhālika ghayra anna al-jawāriya ṭāla bihimu al-kitāfu wa-qad kallat minhumu al-sawāʿidu wa-al-aṭrāfu wa-al-ṣawābu annī aḥulluhum fa-la-rubbamā ṭāla al-ṣirāʿu fī hādhā al-dasti maʿaka
sentences.l: So she laughed and said: I have answered you to that, except that the slave-girls — the pinioning has gone long upon them, and the forearms and the extremities have grown weary in them; and the right-course is that I loose them; for perhaps the wrestling will go long in this bout with you.
sentences.i: She laughed and said: I grant you that. But the girls have been long in their bonds, and their arms and limbs are weary; the best course is that I release them, for the wrestling in this bout with you may well run long.
sentences.n: غَيْرَأَنَّ is printed as one word (ghayra anna, "except that") and kept so. الْكِتَاف I take as the wrestlers' "pinioning", a binding by the shoulders (Lane gives a sense of tying the arms behind the shoulders); the girls have been held in such grips for a long time. This is a technical term and my reading of it is a best fit. In فَلَرُبَّمَا the لَـ is the emphatic lām: "it may well be that". أَجَابَ إِلَى is "to comply with".

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا أَقْبَلَتْ عَلَى الْجَوَارِي وَحَلَّتْ أَكْتَافَهُنَّ وَقَلَٰتْ لَهُنَّ بِلِسَانِ الرُّومِ اِذْهَبْنَ إِلَى مَوْضِعٍ تَأْمَنَّ فِيهِ عَلَى أَنْفُسِكُنَّ حَتَّى يَنْقَطِعَ طَمَعُ هَذَا الْمُسْلِمِ مِنْكُنَّ
sentences.tr: thumma innahā aqbalat ʿalā al-jawārī wa-ḥallat aktāfahunna wa-qālat lahunna bi-lisāni al-Rūmi idhhabna ilā mawḍiʿin taʾmanna fīhi ʿalā anfusikunna ḥattā yanqaṭiʿa ṭamaʿu hādhā al-muslimi minkunna
sentences.l: Then indeed she turned to the slave-girls and loosed their shoulder-bonds, and said to them in the tongue of Rūm: Go to a place in which you are safe upon yourselves, until the greed of this Muslim is cut off from you.
sentences.i: Then she turned to the girls, undid their shoulder-bonds, and said to them in the Greek tongue: Go to some place where you may be safe, until this Muslim's covetous designs on you come to nothing.
sentences.n: The edition prints قلت for قالت; the dagger alif makes it read qālat, "she said" (the same letters could be "I said", but she is the speaker). She speaks Greek to the girls, presumably so that Sharkān cannot follow. تَأْمَنَّ has a doubled nūn because the stem ends in -n and the feminine-plural ending is -na. طَمَع is plain greed, and here it is frankly his lust for the girls that she wants out of the picture. أَقْبَلَ عَلَى is "to turn to, attend to".

sentences.t: فَذَهَبْنَ الْجَوَارِي وَشَرْكَانُ يَنْظُرُ إِلَيْهِنَّ وَهُنَّ يَتَفَرَّجْنَ إِلَيْهِمَا
sentences.tr: fa-dhahabna al-jawārī wa-Sharkānu yanẓuru ilayhinna wa-hunna yatafarrajna ilayhimā
sentences.l: So they went off, the slave-girls, and Sharkān looking at them, and they watching-as-spectacle at the two of them.
sentences.i: So the girls went off, with Sharkān looking after them; and they, for their part, stood watching the pair as at a show.
sentences.n: فَذَهَبْنَ الْجَوَارِي puts the verb in the plural before its plural subject, where Classical Arabic would write ذَهَبَتِ الْجَوَارِي; this agreement is a Middle Arabic habit. يَتَفَرَّجْنَ is "to watch for diversion, as at a spectacle", and here it takes إِلَى.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ دَنَا كُلٌّ مِنْهُمَا بِصَاحِبِهِ وَجَعَلَ بَطْنَهُ عَلَى بَطْنِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma danā kullun minhumā bi-ṣāḥibihi wa-jaʿala baṭnahu ʿalā baṭnihā
sentences.l: Then each of the two drew-near with his companion, and he put his belly upon her belly.
sentences.i: Then the two closed with one another, and he set his belly against hers.
sentences.n: دَنَا بِـ is "to come close with", here "to close with, grapple", and صَاحِبِهِ "his companion" stands for his opponent. The belly-to-belly grip is the wrestlers' close hold, and the comedy of the scene sits in it.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا صَارَتْ بَطْنُهُ عَلَى بَطْنِهَا وَعَلِمَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ مِنْهُ ذَلِكَ رَفَعَتْهُ عَلَى يَدَيْهَا أَسْرَعَ مِنَ الْبَرْقِ الْخَاطِفِ وَرَمَتْهُ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ فَوَقَعَ عَلَى ظَهْرِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ṣārat baṭnuhu ʿalā baṭnihā wa-ʿalimati al-jāriyatu minhu dhālika rafaʿathu ʿalā yadayhā asraʿa mina al-barqi al-khāṭifi wa-ramathu ilā al-arḍi fa-waqaʿa ʿalā ẓahrih
sentences.l: And when his belly became upon her belly, and the girl knew that from him, she lifted him upon her hands, quicker than the snatching lightning, and threw him to the ground, and he fell upon his back.
sentences.i: And when belly lay on belly, and the girl perceived what was in him, she heaved him up on her two hands, swifter than the lightning-flash, and flung him to the ground, and he fell on his back.
sentences.n: صَارَتْ has a feminine ending though بَطْنُهُ is grammatically masculine; either the print treats "belly" as feminine or it slips, and I keep it as printed. ذَلِكَ, "that", is left unnamed. After his confession that her beauty undid him, it is most likely his arousal, or at least his distraction, that she perceives and takes advantage of. أَسْرَعَ is an accusative of state, "swifter than".

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ فَإِنِّي وَهَبْتُكَ رُوحَكَ مَرَّةً ثَانِيَةً فَإِنَّ فِى الْوَجْهِ الْأَوَّلِ أَكْرَمْتُكَ فِيهِ لِأَجْلِ نَبِيِّكَ فَإِنَّهُ مَا أَحَلَّ قَتْلَ النِّسْوَانِ وَفِى الْوَجْهِ الثَّانِي لِأَجْلِ ضَعْفِكَ وَحَدَانَةِ سِنِّكَ وَغُرْبَتِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu fa-innī wahabtuka rūḥaka marratan thāniyatan fa-inna fī al-wajhi al-awwali akramtuka fīhi li-ajli nabiyyika fa-innahu mā aḥalla qatla al-niswāni wa-fī al-wajhi al-thānī li-ajli ḍaʿfika wa-ḥadānati sinnika wa-ghurbatik
sentences.l: So she said to him: For I have given you your soul a second time; for in the first aspect I honoured you in it for the sake of your prophet, for he did not make lawful the killing of women; and in the second aspect, for the sake of your weakness and the youth of your age and your strangerhood.
sentences.i: She said to him: See, I have granted you your life a second time. The first time I spared you for the sake of your prophet, since he did not allow the killing of women; and now it is for the sake of your weakness, your tender years, and your being a stranger here.
sentences.n: فِى is the edition's usual spelling of فِي and is kept. Her reasoning is compressed and I cannot be sure of it: she spared him the first time out of regard for his Prophet, who (she says) forbade the killing of women. The second reason is plainer. وَحَدَانَةِ is printed with ن where the sense wants ث: it is a one-dot misprint for حَدَاثَة, "youth" (حَدَاثَةُ السِّنِّ, "youthfulness"). I point the letters as printed and read the word as ḥadātha. النِّسْوَان is a collective plural, "womenfolk". الْوَجْه, literally "face", is "aspect, respect, ground".

sentences.t: وَلَكِنْ أُوصِيكَ إِنْ كَانَ فِي عَسْكَرُا لْمُسْلِمِينَ الَّذِينَ جَٰأُوا مِنْ عِنْدِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ الَّذِينَ أَرْسَلَهُمْ لِأَجْلِ الْمَلِكِ الْقُسْطَنْطِينِيَّةِ أَقْوَى مِنْكَ فَأَرْسِلْهُ إِلَيَّ وَقُلْ لَهُ عَلَيَّ
sentences.tr: wa-lākin ūṣīka in kāna fī ʿaskaru al-muslimīna alladhīna jāʾū min ʿindi ʿUmara ibni al-Nuʿmāni alladhīna arsalahum li-ajli al-maliki al-Qusṭanṭīniyyati aqwā minka fa-arsilhu ilayya wa-qul lahu ʿalayya
sentences.l: But I charge you: if there be in the army of the Muslims, who came from the presence of ʿUmar son of al-Nuʿmān, whom he sent for the sake of the king of Constantinople, one stronger than you, then send him to me and say to him: Upon me!
sentences.i: But I charge you: if among the army of the Muslims who have come from ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, those he sent on behalf of the king of Constantinople, there be one stronger than you, send him to me and say to him: Come at me!
sentences.n: The edition prints the article's alif on the end of the previous word, عسكرا لمسلمين. I keep the printed division and point it so the letters stand: the alif after the ra is silent and the lām takes a sukūn, so you read ʿaskaru al-muslimīn. جَٰأُوا is printed جأوا (for جاؤوا), and the dagger alif makes it jāʾū. الْمَلِكِ الْقُسْطَنْطِينِيَّةِ puts the article on the first term of the genitive chain, which Classical Arabic avoids. The challenge عَلَيَّ is short for something like "[come] at me"; the print gives no verb, and I read it as a challenge. أَقْوَى is the postponed subject of كَانَ.

sentences.t: فَإِنَّ الْمِصْرَاعَ أَنْوَاعًا وَمَرَاتِبَ وَضُرُوبًا مِثْلَ الْوَهْمِ وَمِنْهَا الْمُسَابَقَةُ وَالْمُنَازَلَةُ وَأَخْذُ الرِّجْلَيْنِ وَعَضُّ الْفَخِذِ وَالْعِرَاكِ وَالشِّبَاكِ
sentences.tr: fa-inna al-miṣrāʿa anwāʿan wa-marātiba wa-ḍurūban mithla al-wahmi wa-minhā al-musābaqatu wa-al-munāzalatu wa-akhdhu al-rijlayni wa-ʿaḍḍu al-fakhidh wa-al-ʿirāki wa-al-shibāk
sentences.l: For the miṣrāʿ — kinds and ranks and sorts, like the supposition; and among them the racing and the single-combat and the taking of the two legs and the biting of the thigh; and the grappling and the nets —
sentences.i: For wrestling has many kinds, degrees and sorts, like fancy itself; among them are racing, single combat, seizing the two legs, biting the thigh, grappling and clinches —
sentences.n: الْمِصْرَاع usually means "door-leaf" (or a verse half-line). I take it as the edition's slip for الْمُصَارَعَة, "wrestling", because the two look alike and the context demands it, but I point the letters as printed. أَنْوَاعًا وَمَرَاتِبَ وَضُرُوبًا stand as accusatives after إِنَّ, which is Middle Arabic. مِثْلَ الْوَهْمِ, "like fancy or supposition", makes no sense in a list of holds and may be corrupt; I give the printed word and flag it. Then come the contest of speed, hand-to-hand fighting, seizing the legs, and biting the thigh. شِبَاك, literally "nets", is used for the entangling holds of the wrestler; the case endings of الْعِرَاكِ وَالشِّبَاكِ are a guess, since the speech is cut off there by Sharkān's reply.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ شَرْكَانُ وَقَدْ زَادَ غَيْظُهُ مِنْهَا وَاللَّهِ يَاسَيِّدَتِي إِذَاكَانَ الْقَيِّمُ الصَّفَدِيُّ أَوِ الْقَيِّمُ مُحَمَّدٌ قَيْمَالُ أَوِ ابْنُ السُّدِّيِّ فِي زَمَانِهِ مَاحَفِظْتُ هَذِهِ الْمَوَالِيفَ الَّتِي ذَكَرْتِهِمْ لِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Sharkānu wa-qad zāda ghayẓuhu minhā wa-Allāhi yāsayyidatī idhākāna al-qayyimu al-Ṣafadiyyu aw al-qayyimu Muḥammadun Qaymālu aw ibnu al-Suddiyyi fī zamānihi māḥafiẓtu hādhihi al-mawālīfa allatī dhakartihim lī
sentences.l: And he said, Sharkān — and his rage at her had increased — By God, O my lady, if there were the steward al-Ṣafadī, or the steward Muḥammad Qaymāl, or Ibn al-Suddī in his time, I have not memorised these mawālīf which you have mentioned them to me.
sentences.i: Then Sharkān, his rage against her grown greater, said: By God, my lady, even were the steward al-Ṣafadī, or the steward Muḥammad Qaymāl, or Ibn al-Suddī alive in his own day, I should not have mastered these tricks you have named to me.
sentences.n: The edition prints اذاكان and ياسيدتي each as one word; both are kept fused. The three names are men of the wrestling world (or perhaps of learning) whom the text does not explain; القَيِّم is a steward or overseer, here almost a title, and the spellings Qaymāl and al-Suddī are our best reading of the print. مَاحَفِظْتُ and the word الْمَوَالِيف are the obscure points: the plural seems to name wrestling holds or tricks, and we take the verb as "I have not memorised", i.e. "I know none of these"; this is a reading, not a certainty. ذَكَرْتِهِمْ "you mentioned them" has the plural pronoun for things, and it is feminine "you" because Sharkān addresses the girl.

sentences.t: وَلَكِنْ بَاسَيِّدَتِي وَاللَّهِ مَا صَرَعْتِنِي بِقُوَّتِكِ وَلَكِنْ لَمَّا رَا وَدَتْنِي إِلَى كَفَلِكِ وَنَحْنُ يَا أَهْلَ الْعِرَاقِ نُحِبُّ الْفَخِذَ الْكَبِيرَ فَمَا بَقِيَ لِي عَقْلٌ وَلَابَصِيرَةٌ
sentences.tr: wa-lākin bāsayyidatī wa-Allāhi mā ṣaraʿtinī bi-quwwatiki wa-lākin lammā rā wadatnī ilā kafaliki wa-naḥnu yā ahla al-ʿirāqi nuḥibbu al-fakhidha al-kabīra fa-mā baqiya lī ʿaqlun wa-lābaṣīra
sentences.l: And but, O-my-lady, by God, you did not throw me by your strength; but when you lured me to your rump — and we, O people of Iraq, love the big thigh — there remained to me no mind and no insight.
sentences.i: But, my lady, by God, it was not your strength that threw me. It was this: when you drew me on toward your backside — and we men of Iraq, you must know, love a big thigh — no wit or sense was left in me.
sentences.n: The edition prints باسيدتي where the sense wants يَا سَيِّدَتِي (the second and third letters are the same shape); it is a slip, kept as printed and pointed bā-sayyidatī, to be read as "O my lady". Likewise را ودتني is راودتني "you solicited me" split in two; both halves are kept, and the second begins with a fatḥa on the wāw. كَفَل is the rump or buttocks. The verbs of address are feminine (صَرَعْتِنِي, بِقُوَّتِكِ), since he is speaking to the girl.

sentences.t: فَإِنْ شِئْتِ تُصَارِعِينَنِي وَفَهْمِي مَعِي فَمَابَقِيَ لِي دَسْتٌ إِلَّا هَذَا بِقَانُونِ هَذِهِ الصِّنَاعَةِ لِأَنَّ نَشَاطِي قَدْ رَجَعَ لِي فِي هَذِهِ السَّاعَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-in shiʾti tuṣāriʿīnanī wa-fahmī maʿī fa-mābaqiya lī dastun illā hādhā bi-qānūni hādhihi al-ṣināʿati li-anna nashāṭī qad rajaʿa lī fī hādhihi al-sāʿa
sentences.l: So if you wish, you wrestle me, and my understanding with me; for there remains to me no bout except this, by the rule of this craft, because my vigour has returned to me in this hour.
sentences.i: So if you will, wrestle me, with my wits about me, for I have only this one bout left, by the rules of this craft, since my strength has come back to me this very hour.
sentences.n: The verb تُصَارِعِينَنِي keeps the feminine-singular nūn (ـِينَ) and adds the nūn of the pronoun; it follows إِنْ شِئْتِ without a subjunctive or jussive, which is the plain Middle Arabic way of saying "if you wish, you wrestle me". دَسْت is the Persian dast, a round or bout of play. فَهْمِي مَعِي, "my understanding is with me", means he is in full possession of his wits this time. مَابَقِيَ is printed as one word.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ كَلَامَهُ قَالَتْ لَهُ مَا تُرِيدُ بِهَذَا الصِّرَاعِ يَامَغْلُوبُ تَعَالَ وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّ هَذَا الدَّسْتَ الْكِفَايَةُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿat kalāmahu qālat lahu mā turīdu bi-hādhā al-ṣirāʿi yāmaghlūbu taʿāla wa-iʿlam anna hādhā al-dasta al-kifāya
sentences.l: And when she heard his speech she said to him: What do you want with this wrestling, O defeated one? Come, and know that this bout — the sufficiency.
sentences.i: When she heard his words she said to him: What do you want of this wrestling, vanquished man? Come, then, and know that this bout will be enough.
sentences.n: الدَّسْتَ الْكِفَايَةُ is loosely built: the bout in the accusative after أَنَّ, then "the sufficiency" as its predicate. We read it as "this bout is the one that suffices", that is, the last. مَا تُرِيدُ بِـ is "what do you intend by", with بِـ introducing what he is after.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا انْحَنَتْ وَطَلَبَتْهُ لِلْمُصْرَاعِ فَانْحَنَى شَرْكَانُ عَلَيْهَا وَأَخَذَ فِى الْجِدِّ وَاحْتَرَزَ مِنَ الْجَذْلَانِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahā inḥanat wa-ṭalabathu li-al-muṣrāʿi fa-inḥanā Sharkānu ʿalayhā wa-akhadha fī al-jiddi wa-iḥtaraza mina al-jadhlān
sentences.l: Then indeed she bent, and sought him for the wrestling; and Sharkān bent upon her, and took to the earnestness, and guarded himself from the glad-one.
sentences.i: Then she bent forward and called him to the bout, and Sharkān bent over her, set to it in earnest, and kept himself on guard against the exultant girl.
sentences.n: لِلْمُصْرَاعِ is printed للمصراع. The letters read most naturally as a noun of the wrestling, muṣrāʿ, which we use; the dictionary word مِصْرَاع, "leaf of a door", does not suit. الْجَذْلَان is "the glad, exultant one", and we take it to be the girl, gleeful at his earlier fall; it may instead be an abstract "gladness". Either way, the point is that he is wary of her this time. أَخَذَ فِي is "set about".

sentences.t: وَتَعَارَكَا سَاعَةً فَوَجَدَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ فِيهِ قُوَّةً لَمْ تَعْهَدْهَا مِنْهُ أَوَّلًا
sentences.tr: wa-taʿārakā sāʿatan fa-wajadati al-jāriyatu fīhi quwwatan lam taʿhadhā minhu awwalan
sentences.l: And the two grappled an hour, and the girl found in him a strength she had not known from him at first.
sentences.i: They grappled for an hour, and the girl found in him a strength that she had not known him to have at first.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ يَامُسْلِمُ أَخَذْتَ لِنَفْسِكَ الْحَذَرَ فَقَالَ لَهَا نَعَمْ وَأَنْتِ تَعْلَمِينَ أَنَّ مَابَقِيَ لِي مَعَكِ غَيْرُ هَذَا الدَّسْتِ وَبَعْدَ هَذَا يَذْهَبُ كُلٌّ مِنَّا فِي طَرِيقِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu yāmuslimu akhadhta li-nafsika al-ḥadhara fa-qāla lahā naʿam wa-anti taʿlamīna anna mābaqiya lī maʿaki ghayru hādhā al-dasti wa-baʿda hādhā yadhhabu kullun minnā fī ṭarīqih
sentences.l: And she said to him: O Muslim, you have taken for yourself the caution. And he said to her: Yes; and you know that there remains to me with you nothing other than this bout, and after this each one of us goes in his road.
sentences.i: Then she said to him: Muslim, you have taken care of yourself! Yes, he said, and you know that I have nothing left to try with you but this one bout, and after it each of us will go his own way.
sentences.n: يَامُسْلِمُ is the girl's mocking address: she, a Byzantine, calls the prince simply "Muslim". أَخَذَ لِنَفْسِهِ الْحَذَرَ is "took precaution for himself", the لِـ marking the person for whom the care is taken. مَابَقِيَ is printed as one word.

sentences.t: فَضَحِكَتْ وَضَحِكَ الْآخَرُ فِي وَجْهِهَا فَلَمَّا وَقَعَ ذَلِكَ سَبَقَتْ إِلَى فَخِذِهِ وَقَبَضَتْهُ عَلَى غَفْلَةٍ مِنْهُ وَأَلْقَتْهُ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ فَوَقَعَ عَلَى ظَهْرِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-ḍaḥikat wa-ḍaḥika al-ākharu fī wajhihā fa-lammā waqaʿa dhālika sabaqat ilā fakhidhihi wa-qabaḍathu ʿalā ghaflatin minhu wa-alqathu ʿalā al-arḍi fa-waqaʿa ʿalā ẓahrih
sentences.l: And she laughed, and the other laughed in her face; and when that occurred, she got ahead to his thigh, and seized him on a heedlessness from him, and threw him on the ground, and he fell on his back.
sentences.i: She laughed, and he laughed back in her face; but when that had passed she darted in upon his thigh, caught him off his guard, and threw him to the ground, and he fell upon his back.
sentences.n: الْآخَر, "the other", is Sharkān, set against الجارية. The edition prints the word with a plain alif; the vocalisation supplies the madda.
